name: ox

attributes.attribute: a bull that is castrated and tamed
large frame used to pull loads
less central than cows or bulls in myth
a grand ridge in western Ireland

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The term turns loose and may fall on full cattle. In strict speak it signifies a bull whose stones are gone, of the tamed flock. A keeper takes a young bull's seed to add flesh, settle a hard temper, and stop rival males from dueling. Such an ox then drags carts and waggons, for the broad ribs grant pull. The same body finishes as a feed. Myth and legend set the one ox beneath the pieces of the cow and the bull, yet it still shows up as grit and staying. Named sites tend to be tall, and Ireland keeps a high ridge in the west that borrows the name of the Ox Mountains.

okr.objective: Set the ox as a castrated draft bull that holds a modest place in myth beside cows and bulls.
key_results: The ox signifies a bull made tame at breeding.
A keeper takes a seed's stones to add flesh and settle the herd.
The ox drags loads on broad ribs.
Myth ranks the ox under the cow and the bull.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
